Description: explicit — omitted glyphs field, text renders in wrong font
prompt: My MapLibre GL JS stylesheet has no `glyphs` property set at all, and my symbol layers have `text-font` set to a font name. Text labels are showing up, but in a generic font, not the one I specified. Is this a bug I need to fix, or expected behavior? What's actually happening?

The `text‑font` array is treated exactly like a CSS `font-family` list: the first name that the browser can find (via a system font or a web‑font you have loaded with `@font-face`) is used. If the font you named isn’t available locally, the browser picks its generic fallback (usually “sans‑serif”), which is why you see a “generic” looking typeface. --- ## What’s really happening under the hood | Situation | What MapLibre does | Result you see | |-----------|-------------------|----------------| | **`glyphs` omitted** (your case) | • No glyph‑PBF server is consulted.
• For each text‑codepoint MapLibre calls **TinySDF** to rasterise the glyph **locally** using the first matching font from the `text-font` list.
• Font resolution follows the same rules the browser uses for CSS `font-family`. | Text appears, but in whatever local/system font the browser could resolve. If the named font isn’t installed or isn’t loaded as a web‑font, you get the generic fallback. | | **`glyphs` present but a specific range fails to load** | Same fallback path is taken *only for the missing range*. The rest of the tile still uses the served SDF glyphs. | You’ll see a mix: most characters look like the intended font, the missing ones look like the generic fallback. | | **`glyphs` present and all ranges load** | MapLibre fetches pre‑computed SDF glyph PBFs from the URL template and renders them directly. | Text looks exactly like the font that was used to generate the PBFs (independent of what’s installed on the client). | > **Key point:** The fallback is **only** a GL JS feature. MapLibre Native does **not** have an equivalent “omit‑glyphs → local‑fonts” mode; it requires a `font-faces` property (see the skill page) or a proper glyph server. --- ## Why you’re seeing a *generic* font 1. **The font name you wrote in `text-font` does not match any locally‑available font.** - Example: `"MyBrand Bold"` but you only have `"MyBrand-Regular"` installed. - The browser’s cascade then falls back to its default `sans-serif`. 2. **The font is a web‑font that you haven’t loaded yet.** - `@font-face` rules (or `document.fonts.load()`) must be in place *before* the map tries to draw the labels. - If the font is still loading when the first tile renders, MapLibre will use the fallback for that frame; later frames will switch once the font is ready. 3. **Case‑sensitivity / whitespace mismatch.** - Font‑family names are compared **exactly** (including spaces). `"Noto Sans"` ≠ `"NotoSans"`. 4. **CJK characters** are a special case (see below). Even if you list a CJK font, GL JS will ignore it unless you disable `localIdeographFontFamily`. --- ## How to get the exact font you want ### 1. Keep the `glyphs` URL (recommended for cross‑platform consistency) ```json { "glyphs": "https://my.cdn.com/fonts/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf", "layers": [ { "type": "symbol", "layout": { "text-font": ["My Brand Regular", "Noto Sans Regular"], "text-field": "{name}" } } ] } ``` *Steps* 1. **Obtain or generate the PBFs** for the font(s) you need. - For common fonts (Noto, Open Sans, Roboto, etc.) you can copy the pre‑built trees from the **openmaptiles/fonts** or **UNDP‑Data/fonts** repos. - For a custom TTF/OTF, run **Font Maker** (`npm i -g @mapbox/font-maker`) or **fontnik** to produce the `{fontstack}/{range}.pbf` files. 2. **Serve them** from a static host that supports CORS (e.g. an S3 bucket, Cloudflare Workers, your own web server). 3. **Make sure the folder names** (`{fontstack}`) exactly match the strings you use in `text-font`. 4. **Test** by opening the network tab – you should see GET requests like `.../My%20Brand%20Regular/0-255.pbf`. *Result*: The map will render the exact glyph shapes you generated, independent of the client’s OS or installed fonts, and the same result will appear on MapLibre Native when you also configure `font-faces`. ### 2. Use the local‑fonts fallback deliberately (when you *don’t* want a glyph server) If you truly want to rely on the client’s installed fonts (e.g. an intranet app where every workstation already has the corporate font), keep `glyphs` omitted **and** make sure the font is available locally: ```html ``` *Things to watch* - **Load order** – the map must be created **after** the font is loaded, otherwise the first render will use the fallback. `document.fonts.ready` (or `font.load()`) guarantees the font is ready. - **CJK characters** – even if you load a CJK web‑font, GL JS will *ignore* it unless you set `localIdeographFontFamily: false`. By default GL JS always rasterises CJK locally with TinySDF, because serving thousands of glyph ranges per tile is prohibitively heavy. - **Cross‑browser differences** – the exact appearance will vary between Chrome, Safari, Edge, etc., because each uses its own rendering engine for the local font. ### 3. Special handling for CJK (Chinese/Japanese/Korean) - **Default** (`localIdeographFontFamily` left at its default `'sans-serif'`): - All ideographs are rendered locally with TinySDF. - `text-font` entries are ignored for those codepoints (only the weight keyword is honoured). - This is fast and avoids massive glyph‑PBF traffic. - **If you *must* use a specific CJK font** (e.g. corporate Noto CJK SC): ```javascript const map = new maplibregl.Map({ container: 'map', style: 'my-style.json', localIdeographFontFamily: '"Noto Sans CJK SC", sans-serif' // optional custom on‑device font }); ``` - **Or** disable the local‑ideograph optimisation entirely (slow, many requests): ```javascript const map = new maplibregl.Map({ container: 'map', style: 'my-style.json', localIdeographFontFamily: false // forces glyph‑PBF fetch for CJK }); ``` - **Note:** Disabling it is rarely needed; the default local rendering is usually acceptable for most maps. ### 4. Wait for the font to load before creating the map. | | **CJK** | Leave `localIdeographFontFamily` at its default (fast, local rendering). Change only if you have a specific on‑device CJK font you want to use. | | **Arabic / Hebrew** | Load the RTL plugin (`setRTLTextPlugin`). | | **MapLibre Native** | The above fallback does **not** work; you must use the `font-faces` property and serve glyph PBFs. | --- ## Common pitfalls & how to diagnose them | Symptom | Likely cause | How to verify | |---------|--------------|---------------| | Labels appear, but in *Helvetica* or *Arial* instead of `"My Brand"` | Font not loaded or name mismatch. | Open DevTools → **Elements** → inspect a label’s computed `font-family`. If you need the same appearance on MapLibre Native, go with option **(b)** and also configure the `font-faces` property on the native side. Otherwise, for a pure‑web, offline‑friendly map, the local‑fonts mode works fine—just make sure the font is truly available to the browser.

Description: implicit — offline/local fonts on MapLibre Native, not GL JS
prompt: I'm building an offline map app with MapLibre Native on Android and want labels to render in local device fonts without running a glyphs server. What's the right way to configure this?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
## TL;DR  
**MapLibre Native (Android) cannot fall back to a remote glyph server when `glyphs` is missing.**  
To render labels completely offline you must:

1. **Bundle the font files you want to use** (e.g. Noto Sans, Noto Sans CJK SC, Noto Sans Arabic) in your app’s `assets/` folder.  
2. **Add a top‑level `font‑faces` array** to the style JSON that maps each `text‑font` name to one (or more) local font files and declares the Unicode ranges those files cover.  
3. **Tell the native SDK to use a `FontManager` that can read the `local://` URLs** you put in `font‑faces`.  
4. (Optional) **Bundle pre‑generated glyph‑PBFs** if you prefer the SDF‑pipeline over on‑the‑fly SDF generation – but this is *not required* when you use `font‑faces`.  

Below is a step‑by‑step guide, code snippets, and a checklist of gotchas.

---

## 1. Why `font‑faces` and not `glyphs`?

| Feature | `glyphs` (remote PBF) | `font‑faces` (local fonts) |
|---------|----------------------|----------------------------|
| **Offline** | ❌ Needs a reachable HTTP server | ✅ Fonts live in the APK |
| **CJK handling** | You would have to ship huge PBF trees (many ranges) | One CJK font file covers the whole ideograph block |
| **Version support** | All MapLibre Native releases | Android ≥ **11.13.0** (iOS ≥ 6.18.0) |
| **GL JS vs Native** | GL JS can fall back to TinySDF when a glyph PBF fails (≥ 5.11) | Native **does not** have that fallback – you must supply `font‑faces` or a glyph server |
| **Shaping** | Only SDF glyphs → no complex shaping (Devanagari, Khmer, etc.) | Same limitation – the engine still maps one code‑point → one glyph. (RTL still needs the RTL plugin on GL JS; Native has no built‑in shaping.) |

> **Bottom line:** For a truly offline Android map you *must* use `font‑faces`. Omitting `glyphs` alone will not make Native render text.

---

## 2. Bundle the fonts

1. **Pick the fonts** you need. The safest universal choice is the Noto family:
   * `NotoSans-Regular.ttf` – Latin, Greek, Cyrillic, etc.
   * `NotoSansArabic-Regular.ttf` – Arabic & Hebrew (RTL)
   * `NotoSansSC-Regular.otf` – Simplified Chinese (CJK)
   * `NotoSansTC-Regular.otf` – Traditional Chinese (CJK)
   * `NotoSansJP-Regular.otf` – Japanese (CJK)
   * `NotoSansKR-Regular.otf` – Korean (CJK)
   * Add any brand‑specific font you want to use.

2. **Copy them into the APK assets folder** (any sub‑folder works, e.g. `src/main/assets/fonts/`).

   ```
   app/
   └─ src/
      └─ main/
         └─ assets/
            └─ fonts/
               ├─ NotoSans-Regular.ttf
               ├─ NotoSansArabic-Regular.ttf
               ├─ NotoSansSC-Regular.otf
               └─ …
   ```

3. **(Optional) Reduce size** – if you only need a subset of Unicode, you can create a “subset” TTF with tools like `pyftsubset` or FontForge. The `unicode-range` you declare later must match the subset.

---

## 3. Add a `font‑faces` block to your style JSON

The `font-faces` property lives **at the top level** of the style (same level as `version`, `sources`, `layers`, …).  
Each entry has three required fields:

| Field | Meaning |
|-------|---------|
| `font-family` | The exact string you will use in `text-font` arrays. |
| `src` | One or more URLs that point to the font file. For Android assets use the `local://` scheme (`local://fonts/…`). |
| `unicode-range` | A comma‑separated list of Unicode ranges that this file covers. Use the `U+xxxx-xxxx` syntax. |

### Minimal example (offline, Noto Sans + CJK)

```json
{
  "version": 8,
  "glyphs": "",                     // can be omitted or left empty – Native will ignore it
  "font-faces": [
    {
      "font-family": "Noto Sans",
      "src": ["local://fonts/NotoSans-Regular.ttf"],
      "unicode-range": "U+0000-00FF, U+0100-024F, U+0370-03FF, U+0400-04FF"
    },
    {
      "font-family": "Noto Sans CJK SC",
      "src": ["local://fonts/NotoSansSC-Regular.otf"],
      "unicode-range": "U+4E00-9FFF, U+3400-4DBF, U+20000-2A6DF, U+2A700-2B73F"
    },
    {
      "font-family": "Noto Sans Arabic",
      "src": ["local://fonts/NotoSansArabic-Regular.ttf"],
      "unicode-range": "U+0600-06FF, U+0750-077F, U+08A0-08FF, U+FB50-FDFF, U+FE70-FEFF"
    }
  ],
  "layers": [
    {
      "id": "place-labels",
      "type": "symbol",
      "source": "osm",
      "source-layer": "place",
      "layout": {
        "text-field": ["get", "name"],
        "text-font": ["Noto Sans", "Noto Sans CJK SC", "Noto Sans Arabic"],
        "text-size": 12,
        "text-anchor": "center"
      },
      "paint": {
        "text-color": "#222"
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

**Key points**

* **Order matters** – `text-font` is a fallback list. The first entry whose `unicode-range` contains the code‑point is used.
* **CJK fonts**: you can list a single CJK font that covers all ideographs you need. The engine will still generate SDF on‑the‑fly from the TTF/OTF, so you don’t need the massive glyph‑PBF tree that a remote server would require.
* **RTL scripts**: the above Arabic entry will give you the correct glyph shapes, but **Native does not perform RTL reordering**. If you need proper Arabic/Hebrew you must pre‑shape the text (e.g. with ICU’s `Bidi` and `ArabicShaping` utilities) before feeding it to `text-field`, or accept left‑to‑right rendering.

---

## 4. Tell the SDK to use a `FontManager`

MapLibre Native ships a default `FontManager` that knows how to resolve `local://` URLs. You just need to instantiate it (or use the singleton) **before** the map is created.

### Kotlin example (Android)

```kotlin
import org.maplibre.android.maps.MapLibre
import org.maplibre.android.maps.MapView
import org.maplibre.android.maps.Style
import org.maplibre.android.maps.FontManager

class MainActivity : AppCompatActivity() {

    private lateinit var mapView: MapView

    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)

        // 1️⃣ Initialise the SDK (once per process)
        MapLibre.getInstance(this)

        // 2️⃣ Register a FontManager that can read assets
        MapLibre.getInstance(this).fontManager = FontManager(this)

        // 3️⃣ Inflate your layout that contains a MapView
        setContentView(R.layout.activity_main)
        mapView = findViewById(R.id.mapView)

        mapView.getMapAsync { mapboxMap ->
            // 4️⃣ Load the offline style (stored in assets/style.json)
            mapboxMap.setStyle(
                Style.Builder()
                    .fromUri("asset://style.json")   // <-- our JSON with font-faces
            )
        }
    }

    // Remember to forward lifecycle events to the MapView …
}
```

* `FontManager(this)` automatically maps `local://` to `context.assets`.  
* If you keep the fonts in a different location (e.g. external storage), you can subclass `FontManager` and override `openFontFile(uri: String): InputStream?`.

### Java equivalent

```java
MapLibre.getInstance(this).setFontManager(new FontManager(this));
```

---

## 5. What about CJK and the `localIdeographFontFamily` option?

* **`localIdeographFontFamily` exists only in MapLibre GL JS.**  
* In Native you *must* provide a font that covers the ideographs via `font-faces`. The engine will rasterize those glyphs on‑the‑fly, just like GL JS does when it falls back to TinySDF.
